summary: A2A state strings are owned solely by skein/states.py. Call sites derive via call-time accessors (is_failure_state, is_terminal_state, is_valid_state, all_states, failure_states_sql/sql_in) rather than value-importing sets or spelling literals. tests/test_states.py enforces this structurally (AST literal scan) and behaviourally (synthetic state injection).
problem: The CHANGELOG advertised skein/states.py as the "single source of truth for A2A task state strings" but it was a facade. validator.py re-declared all seven states as an independent frozenset, and the failure triple ('failed','rejected','canceled') was hardcoded at nine call sites across failures/detector.py, dashboard/routes.py and skein_mcp/tools.py. detector.py imported FAILURE_STATES/TERMINAL_STATES behind a `# noqa: F401` while using neither name — an import placed purely to simulate derivation. Adding a state to states.py would have silently missed every one of those sites.
why_chosen: Two properties were needed. First, SQL sites cannot bind a variable-length IN-clause with placeholders cleanly, so they need a rendered fragment: failure_states_sql() builds it from the module-level set at call time, sorted for deterministic SQL text and shape-checked against a regex so a future state string can never become an injection vector. Second, and less obvious: a plain `from ..states import FAILURE_STATES` snapshots the set at module import, so monkeypatching states.py at runtime does not reach it and the drift-guard test cannot detect breakage. Routing every membership check and list render through a call-time accessor makes the whole system observably derived, which is what lets the behavioural test prove derivation instead of merely asserting it. Deriving in _demo_data.py too means the structural scan needs zero carve-outs, and a rule with no exemptions is much harder to erode than one with a precedent for exceptions.
what_we_tried: Verified the guard is not vacuous by mutation: re-hardcoding a single detector.py IN-clause back to ('failed','rejected','canceled') fails both the structural scan and the propagation test.
tradeoffs: Call-time accessors cost a function call per check (irrelevant at this scale) and are slightly less direct to read than a bare set membership. The structural AST scan is a lint-shaped test living in the test suite, which some would argue belongs in a ruff custom rule; ruff cannot express "this literal must come from that module", so the test suite is the only place it can live. Deriving states in _demo_data.py makes the synthetic payloads marginally less literal-readable as sample A2A traffic.

alternatives.option: Leave validator.py's independent frozenset and just add a test asserting it equals ALL_STATES
alternatives.reason_rejected: Catches drift in that one set but does nothing for the nine hardcoded SQL/membership sites, which were the actual bug.
Reads as derived but snapshots at module import; runtime state injection cannot reach it, so the guard test would pass vacuously while real drift went undetected.

alternatives.option: Parameterised IN-clause built from '?' placeholders at each site
alternatives.reason_rejected: Every call site would rebuild the placeholder string and thread the params through, re-introducing per-site logic that can drift. A single rendered fragment keeps the knowledge in one place.

alternatives.option: Structural AST literal scan only, no behavioural test
alternatives.reason_rejected: Proves nobody spells a literal, but not that the derived plumbing actually carries a new state end-to-end (e.g. it would miss the value-import snapshot problem entirely).

constraints_created: No module outside skein/states.py may spell an A2A task state as a string literal — import the constant or use a call-time accessor.

Runtime membership/rendering of states must go through call-time accessors (is_failure_state, is_terminal_state, is_valid_state, all_states, failure_states_sql), never a module-import-time value copy.
State IN-clauses in SQL must be built with states.failure_states_sql() or states.sql_in(), never hand-written.

summary: Cascade detection keeps both signals but stops claiming both are deterministic. Signal 1 (referenceTaskIds) is deterministic and gains an ordering constraint; signal 2 (same-contextId within 300s) is documented as a heuristic lead. The existing `via` label is the honest interface and the README now leads with it.
problem: README:20 advertised "Cascade detection is deterministic, not heuristic", and detector.py's docstring said "Two signals (deterministic, both per A2A spec)". Signal 2 is same-contextId failures inside a 300-second magic window — a temporal correlation guess, as its own docstring conceded by describing results as "plausibly affected". Separately, signal 1 had no time filter and no state filter, so a task that referenced X an hour before X failed was reported as cascade-affected by it.
why_chosen: Deleting the context signal would lose real diagnostic value — co-failure inside one A2A conversation usually does share a root cause, and it is often the only signal available when agents do not populate referenceTaskIds. Silently keeping it while calling it deterministic was the actual defect, and the fix was documentation, not removal, because the code already exposed the distinction through the per-row `via: reference|context|reference+context` label. For the ordering bug, the principled constraint is causal: a task that had already reached a terminal state before the root's terminal_at cannot have been affected by that failure, so exclude it. Deliberately did NOT add a failure-state filter to signal 1: a task that referenced the failure and still completed is part of the lineage story, and the shipped demo/screenshot depends on exactly that case (task-research-notify completes while appearing in the cascade). When the root has no terminal_at there is no instant to order against, so no filter applies.
tradeoffs: The README is longer and less punchy than "deterministic, not heuristic" — a marketing line traded for an accurate one. The ordering constraint relies on terminal_at being populated correctly at ingest; tasks with a missing or clock-skewed terminal_at will not be filtered (they fall through to the no-filter path, which is the safe direction: over-report rather than hide). The 300s window remains a magic default, now at least documented as arbitrary.

alternatives.option: Drop the same-contextId signal entirely so the deterministic claim becomes true
alternatives.reason_rejected: Throws away the only cascade signal available when agents do not populate referenceTaskIds; the problem was the claim, not the signal.

alternatives.option: Add a failure-state filter to signal 1 to match signal 2
alternatives.reason_rejected: A task that referenced the failed task and still completed is genuine lineage; filtering it would gut the demo's headline cascade view.

alternatives.option: Filter signal 1 by referencing-message time >= root terminal_at
alternatives.reason_rejected: Breaks the common and legitimate case where B references A up front, A fails later, and B is then affected. Task terminality, not message time, is the correct causal boundary.

alternatives.option: Make the 300s window configurable in config.json
alternatives.reason_rejected: Already a cascade_for() keyword argument; promoting it to user config adds a knob without a demonstrated need.

constraints_created: Do not describe cascade detection as purely deterministic — the context signal is a documented heuristic and must be labelled as such wherever it is advertised.
Cascade signal 1 must not filter by the referencing task's final state; only by the causal ordering constraint (already-terminal-before-root-failed is excluded).
